The words beginning with “by separation for a moment from whom” are connected with the word “by Him I am now deprived,” occurring in the seventh verse. An example of even the dear becoming undesirable is “with life” [the life-breath]. “This” refers to father and so forth.

He recalls the favors of Śrī Kṛṣṇa—beginning with “by whose shelter” in ten [verses]. By whose shelter, by force; “by Smara”—by Kāma, desire—the power of the extremely proud was taken away as if by grasping the bow alone. Afterwards that bow was made ready too. By it the fish revolving atop the device was pierced. Then, having conquered them, Kṛṣṇā, Draupadī, was obtained.

“U” expresses astonishment. “Khāṇḍava” is Indra’s forest; “I gave [it] to Agni”—I gave it. The assembly hall made by Maya, who was saved in the burning of Khāṇḍava, was obtained; [it was] of wonderful architectural form. “In that sacrifice”—in the Rājasūya sacrifice.

The following verse is not recited [in some readings], nevertheless it is explained. Jarāsandha, whose feet were worshiped by the heads of kings, was killed by your younger brother Bhīma for the sake of the sacrifice; without his defeat the Rājasūya sacrifice would not be possible. He whose being, enthusiasm-power, prowess and strength were like those of ten thousand elephants. Having killed him, the kings whom Mahābhairava, lord of the Pramathas, had brought for his sacrifice, and whom he released, brought tribute to the sacrifice because they had been released.

By whom—the cheaters, Duḥśāsana and the others—your wife’s hair-lock, having been loosened and scattered, was touched and dragged; their wives became husbandless. Therefore, because of widowhood, [he] made [them] loose-haired. What sort of hair-lock? By the great consecration arranged in connection with the Rājasūya sacrifice, it was most praiseworthy; beautiful. At the remembrance of which, when remembering Śrī Kṛṣṇa—obtained at that very time by our mercy—the tears of the wife, which had fallen at His feet, [were] from her mouth. Although the word “fallen” depends on “feet,” it is compounded with “tears” because of their constant mutual dependence.

The one who eats before ten thousand disciples in their row—because of Durvāsā, and because of the unbearable hardship characterized by a curse, created by the enemy Duryodhana—having come to the forest, protected us from that danger. Having done what? Having eaten only the vegetable food, using up the remnant in that very vessel. Because of its being eaten, the assembly of sages, immersed in water, considered the three worlds satisfied.

Thus indeed there is a story in the Mahābhārata: Once Durvāsā was entertained as a guest by Duryodhana. When, being pleased, he said, “Choose a boon,” Duryodhana, having formed in his mind, “May the Pāṇḍavas be destroyed by Durvāsā’s curse,” said: “Yudhiṣṭhira is the chief of our family. Therefore you should also be his guest in exactly this way, accompanied by ten thousand disciples; but you should go to his house after Draupadī has eaten, so that she may not suffer from hunger.” Then, when Durvāsā arrived in just that way, Yudhiṣṭhira, with the highest honor, requested the assembly of sages, “After performing your midday rites, please come,” and the assembly plunged into the water for the Adhamarṣaṇa rite. There, merely remembered by the distressed Draupadī, Śrī Kṛṣṇa immediately came, leaving Rukmiṇī seated on His lap, out of affection for devotees. When she reported the event, the Lord said, “O Draupadī! I too am hungry. First feed Me.” She replied with great embarrassment: “Lord, the inexhaustible food in the vessel given by the sun was eaten by me, after feeding everyone, up to my own meal; therefore there is no food.” Even so, with great insistence, having brought the vessel, He tasted a little vegetable food clinging to it and said, “By this, may the Lord, the self of the universe, be pleased.” Then He sent Bhīma: “Now invite the assembly of sages to eat.” And they, by that much, were completely satisfied and fled out of fear of eating in vain.

Having been astonished, together with Girijā, [Lord Śiva] gave his own Pāśupata weapon. The other guardians of the worlds also gave their own weapons. He states another wonder: “By this”—the great [one], half of Indra’s seat.

“There itself”—in heaven. “While staying as a guest” [with] Gāṇḍīva as the mark; that [is, the arms] whose mark is Gāṇḍīva. “The enemies” are the demons called Nivātakavacas; [the gods] resorted to [my arms] for their killing. By whom [the arms] were made endowed with power. O Ājamīḍha, Yudhiṣṭhira. By Him I am now deprived, bereft. “By the Supreme”—by abiding in His own greatness.

The three verses beginning with “whose friend” are also connected with the preceding “I am deprived by Him” [verse 13]. Being alone, a friend of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, I crossed the ocean of the Kaurava army, whose end was absent in depth and whose far shore was distant, at the seizure of the northern cows. In it were beings difficult to cross, such as Timiṅgila, in the forms of Bhīṣma and the others. The cattle taken away by the enemies were brought back. And from the heads of the enemies, after bewildering them with the bewildering weapon, much wealth—the source of brilliance, in the form of turbans and jewel-studded crowns—was taken. [This was done] by me, as the friend of Kṛṣṇa.

The excellent kings, immense and without limit, whose armies were adorned with circles of chariots, in the armies of Bhīṣma and the others, while He remained beyond my sight in the form of a charioteer. O Lord! He who, by a mere glance, took away the life and so forth of the commanders of the chariot-hosts. “Minds” means power such as enthusiasm. “Saha” means strength. “Ojas” means skill in weapons and so forth.

Then in the sixteenth [chapter], in the dialogue of Earth and Dharma, both afflicted by Kali, the attainment of the protector Parīkṣit is described. “By the instruction of the best of the twice-born”—by good instruction. “At the birth”—at his birth. “Expert in what is born”—knowers of the birth rites. O brāhmaṇa! “In whom are great qualities”—he in whom great qualities are.

“Janamejaya and others”—the excess of a syllable is metrical. In the reading “producing,” the present-participle suffix is used in the sense of cause. The construction of the sentence is: he married in order to beget sons.
“Performed”—that is the meaning of ājahāra. “Śāradvata”—Kṛpa. “In which”—in which Aśvamedha sacrifices—the gods became visible.
“Nijagrāha” means restrained or punished. He points out Kali himself: “the king.”
“For what reason?” This is the meaning: for what reason did he merely seize Kali, and not kill him? Because he is a śūdra, extremely contemptible. “Who struck the cow with his foot.”

“Of this Viṣṇu”—the nectar of the lotus feet of this Viṣṇu. Those who lick and taste it—of those good or great persons, “the support of the topics” is the remainder of the compound. Then let it be spoken.

If not, what [use is there] in other conversations with the untrue [topics], by which life is wasted in vain? Even our effort in this sacrifice is only for drinking the nectar of Hari’s narration—thus he says in one and a half verses. “Small” means short, whose lifespan is [short]; therefore, of mortals, those whose nature is death. Nevertheless, [we are] desirous of the true [and] liberation.

“He who is death”—he was invited in this sacrifice for the Śāmitra rite, the act of killing the animal, for the purpose of restraining death. What then? To this he says, “no one.” What further? To this he says, “Alas! In the human world, let the nectar of Hari’s pastimes—the words—be drunk,” for this purpose. “That in which there is only Hari’s pastime.”

In the absence of that, life is indeed in vain, he says. “Of the dull”—of the lazy. At night, whatever lifespan is ours is taken by sleep. And by day, whatever [time] is ours is taken away by useless actions.

Here then he speaks of the context of punishing Kali—beginning with “when.” When he heard that Kali had entered the country protected by his own army, he then heard that unpleasant news, and somewhat pleasant because it provided the opportunity for the delight of battle; thereafter he took up his bow for the purpose of punishing the wicked. “A śauṇḍa in battle” means skilled in war. In another reading, “śauri in battle” means Śauri, equal to Kṛṣṇa.
Then he departed for conquest of the directions.

“Bhadrāśva and the others” are regions joined to the ocean in the east, west, south and north. Ilāvṛta is on all sides of Mount Meru. Then to the north are Ramyaka and Hiraṇmaya; to the south are Hari-varṣa and Kimpuruṣa.
“The glory being sung.” Hearing the glories and so forth, he gave to them; this is connected with the third [line].

Then in the seventeenth [chapter], the punishment of Kali is spoken, and the extraordinary renunciation of the king, although he possessed such power, is spoken. “Being killed” means being struck or beaten.

“Lotus stalk” is the lotus root, therefore white. “From fear, urinating.” By “as if,” Dharma, remaining with one leg, is shown as if urinating from fear, trembling because his remaining portion is diminishing at every moment through inability to sustain it.

“Yielding dharma”—a giver of oblation. “Emaciated”—thin. “Grass”—herbage. Here, through the destruction of the production of crops and so forth, [she is] like one bereft of a calf. Through the absence of sacrifices and so forth [she is] emaciated. Therefore Earth is indicated as desiring her share of the sacrifice.
“Kārtasvara” is gold. “Whose equipment is made of that”—whose accessories are made of gold; that is the meaning, bound or embossed with gold. “With the bow made ready.”
“You kill” means you cause [them] to be killed. If [he says], “I am a king,” to that he says: by dress alone you are a man-god, like an actor; by conduct, however, you are a non-twice-born śūdra.
“Those not to be lamented”—the innocent ones whom you strike secretly. He is to be lamented; he is guilty; therefore he deserves to be killed.
He addresses the bull: “Who are you?” Or, “you”—he addresses you himself. Are you some god who, existing in the form of a bull, is causing us distress?
“Protected by arms” means protected as if embraced by arms. “Your tears”—without the tears of others, your tears do not fall; thus the cause of distress is shown.

Having said thus, he again addresses the lamenting bull: “O son of Surabhi, do not grieve”—do not lament; “may it go away”—may it depart. He addresses the cow: “O mother, while I, the ruler, am alive, your good alone [will be]; therefore do not cry.”

“I shall kill this one only for my welfare, not for your benefit”—thus he speaks in the two [verses] beginning with “whose.” “O chaste one”—the meaning is: all whatsoever [people]. “Are terrified by the wicked” means are afflicted by them. “Bhaga” is fortune. “Gati” is the next world.
Again he addresses the lamenting bull: “Who cut off”—who severed. “Like you”—those of your kind who are afflicted.
“May there be good for you.” The one who made deformity in your person by cutting off your legs, and thus disgraces the fame, is named.

“When he has been named, how can there be good?” To this he says: Since whoever inflicts harm and suffering on a blameless person, fear of me, such as I am, arises everywhere, therefore there will indeed be good for the virtuous.

Do not think, “I am unable to punish this one”; thus he says, “the offenseless ones.” “Āgaskṛt” is an offender. I shall take away the arm even of an immortal god. By “with the arm-ornament” it is shown that I shall uproot and take it from the root.

Then in the eighteenth [chapter], the brāhmaṇa’s curse of that king is described. And that curse itself became a blessing for him, producing detachment. In order to speak of Parīkṣit’s departure, and to establish that wonder, he recalls the wonder of his birth: “he who…” “Burned” means having been scorched.

From Takṣaka, arising from the anger of a brāhmaṇa, came the disturbance or destruction of life; from that, whatever great fear there was—because of that he was not bewildered. The reason is: his mind was offered to Bhagavān alone.
But “having abandoned” [means this]. Being a disciple of Vaiyāsaki, Śuka. He by whom the truth of the position of Ajita Hari was understood.
Nor is this surprising, he says. Those in whom the topics of Uttamaśloka alone [are found]—therefore, for those who constantly relish the nectar in the form of His story, there is no bewilderment.
In that king, even more, this is not surprising—so he says, “as long as.” “The son of Abhimanyu”—the sole king, the emperor, the lord, as long as [he is ruler].

“Then let there be no entry of Kali; even if he entered here, he did not prevail”—how is that? To this he says, “on that day.” “Yarhi”—in that very moment. “Earth.” “Anuvṛttaḥ”—entered. “In which there is the source of irreligion.”

“Since Kali is the cause of irreligion, why did he not kill him altogether?” To this he says, “does not hate.” “Sāraṅga” is one who takes the essence, like a bee. He states the essence: in which auspicious, meritorious acts bear fruit quickly by mere intention; the other sinful acts do not quickly succeed. Those [sinful acts] succeed only when actually done, not merely when intended.

“Since faults are abundant, hatred alone is appropriate.” No, because among the steady he does nothing; thus he says, “what indeed [would be the use]?” What would come of him? [He is] among the childish and unsteady. Being vigilant and attentive, he behaves like a wolf.
“Pārīkṣitam”—the account concerning Parīkṣit. “You asked”—you inquired.

To say no more, he states the essence of the meaning of all scriptures: “whatever [topics].” The many acts of Him that are to be spoken, concerning His qualities and deeds. By those desiring to become good, desiring true welfare.

For the purpose of speaking again at length, they praise the words of Sūta and their connection, with three [verses] beginning “O Sūta.” “Live for eternal years”—for endless years. The second case is used in the sense of complete connection. “You proclaim pure fame.” And that is nectar for us mortals, warding off death.

Moreover, in this ritual, in this sacrifice, there is no certainty, it is not reliable, because of the abundance of defects and the absence of certainty of result. “Those whose selves are smoky”—us whose bodies are discolored by smoke. The genitive case is used in relation to the ritual. “Āsava” means nectar. “Madhu” means sweet.

“Associates of Bhagavān”—devotees of Viṣṇu. “The association of them”—even its moment, a very small period of time; even with that we do not compare heaven, we do not regard it as equal. Nor liberation [apunarbhava]. The imperative is used in the sense of possibility. What need be said of the insignificant blessings of mortals, beginning with kingship—we do not compare them.

Having thus praised the association of the good, they reveal eagerness to hear: “who indeed?” “A knower of rasa”—one who knows rasa. “In the story of Him who is the ultimate refuge, exclusively, of the greatest beings.” “Without qualities”—without material qualities. The limit of His auspicious qualities even the lords of yoga—whose foremost are Bhava, Śiva, and Pādma, Brahmā—did not reach; they did not count them as having an end.
“Among us, Bhagavān is chief, whose service is to be rendered; you are that [person]. May you expand Hari’s deeds for us who desire to hear.”

When the king had sat for the fast unto death on the Ganges, surrounded by yogic persons, the arrival of Śuka there is spoken of in the nineteenth [chapter]. Thinking of that act done by himself—the throwing of a serpent on the sage’s shoulder—as blameworthy and censurable, he became very distressed. He states the thought with one and a half verses: “Alas!” “Low” means sinful. In the reading amīva, the meaning is the same. “In a brāhmaṇa” means in a brāhmaṇa; “in whom splendor is hidden” means in one whose splendor is concealed.

“What was done”—the sin of disrespecting God, meaning the sin of disregarding the Lord. “From that, let calamity come to me”; but let it be soon, not after a long time; and directly to me, not through a son or another—this is the prayer. “At will” means without restriction. The purpose of the prayer is atonement for the sin, so that he may not do this again.

Having thus directly prayed for calamity to himself, before that he prays for something: “Let the fire that is the angered brāhmaṇa community burn my kingdom and so forth today itself.” The meaning is: may my understanding not again arise for afflicting brāhmaṇas and others.

Thinking thus, the king heard from the sage’s son that on the seventh day death would occur, in the form of destruction. Having heard it from the disciple sent by Śamīka, he considered Takṣaka’s poison-fire good, because it is a cause of detachment for one who is attached to worldly objects.

Then, immediately, having considered both worlds—this and the next—beforehand, even sovereignty, as things to be abandoned, he abandoned them, considering service to Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s feet alone and knowing it as the beginning of all human goals. He sat for the fast in that [place]—that is the meaning. He sat with that resolve. Or, “fast” means a supreme refuge, so that it becomes a supreme resort.

He states the result of the qualifier “on the immortal river.” The Ganges, whose shining beauty is mixed with Tulasī, is the carrier of water made most excellent by the dust from Kṛṣṇa’s feet. In both ways, inside and outside, she purifies the worlds together with Śeṣa and the guardians of the worlds. “About to die” means near death; because the time of death is uncertain, everyone is thus. Therefore who would not serve her?

Having thus definitely decided upon the fast unto death on the Ganges, the path of Viṣṇu: “Pāṇḍaveya” shows the appropriateness of his family. “One whose disposition is nowhere else.” Why? “With the vow of a sage”—peaceful. From what? “By whom all association is released”—he is released from all association.

There, at that time, sages came for the purpose of seeing him, not for bathing at a holy place, because they were fulfilled. “But pilgrimage by such persons is also seen”—to this he says, “generally”: under the pretext of pilgrimage.
Aruṇa and the others are specified separately by the special rank of kāṇḍarṣis. The various ārṣeyas are the gotras of the sages; among them, the foremost. He bowed, touching the earth with his head.

Again he bowed for the purpose of making a request. “One whose mind is secluded”—whose mind is pure. “With hands joined”—he whose two hands were joined. He informed them whether his own intended act—fasting unto death and so forth—was proper or improper.

Having perceived favor through their approval, he praises himself: “Indeed!” Those whose conduct is deserving of favor by the greatest among kings. This is very rare among kings, he says. According to the Smṛti, from the washing of brāhmaṇas’ feet, from the water used to wash their feet, remnants, stool, urine and foot-water should be cast far away; indeed they are discarded far away by them. Then “even farther”—cast away farther still, thrown away; the meaning is that it is unfit even to stand there. He speaks referring to himself, whose act is blameworthy.

“Let the favor be aside for now; even the brāhmaṇa’s curse arose solely from the Lord’s grace”—thus he says. “Of that very blameworthy act”; therefore, of me, sinful and attached in mind to household affairs, the Lord of all higher and lower beings, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Himself, became a brāhmaṇa’s curse for my attainment of Him. When that curse is present, one who is attached to household affairs becomes fearful and disillusioned. Because it has detachment as its root, it has detachment as the cause of attainment. Since detachment is the means by which he is attained, and fear is the root of that [detachment], He caused the brāhmaṇa’s curse for that purpose.

He prays to them with the two [verses] beginning “him”: “Let them recognize me, who have come to Him and taken refuge. And let the goddess Ganges, in divine form, recognize [me].” The word “vā” indicates indifference to the alternative. “Gāthās” means stories.

Obeisance to Śrī Gaṇeśa.

In the Second [Canto], with ten chapters, the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata is described from the beginning. In another book there is an additional verse at the beginning: “I worship that eternal, supremely blissful Hari-Nara, whose name-chanting is the good fruit of gifts, austerity, yoga and the like.”

It is briefly described through statements of the subject and the definition. “Subject” is the naming of the object by name alone. “Definition” is that by which it is indicated and known, namely, the statement of an uncommon characteristic.

But in the First Chapter, through chanting, hearing and the like, concentration of the mind on the gross form of Bhagavān is described.

“I worship that eternal, supremely blissful Hari-Nara, whose name-chanting is the good fruit of gifts, austerity, yoga and the like.”

Now the explanation of the Second Canto. Previously the introduction, together with its context, and Śuka’s arrival were stated. “The wise know an introduction to be [that which is made] for accomplishing the intended purpose.” An introduction is, after mentally grasping the meaning to be presented, the description of another meaning for that purpose.

The sage Śuka then speaks the duty of men asked by the king.

He praises the king’s question with “glorious.” This question, asked by you among the things to be heard and so forth by men, is the supreme question concerning the highest object, and is glorious. For this is beneficial to the world, because it is a cause of liberation. It is approved by knowers of the self and by liberated persons, because of this.

The things stated at the end of the First Canto beginning with “what is to be heard and what is to be chanted” are intended.

Here, for now, while stating the capacity of natural activities to cause misfortune, he gives, in three [verses] beginning with “what is to be heard and so forth,” the answer to “Tell me what is the contrary” [Bhāgavata 1.19.30]. [He speaks] of those attached to houses, and therefore house-dwellers, devoted to the five slaughter places situated in them. The root medh is in the sense of harming.

The five slaughter places of a householder are the hearth, the grinding stone, the implements, the pounding mortar and the water-pot; and what is killed while carrying.

And through those things to be heard and so forth life is wasted in vain, he says. At night, the lifespan that is [spent] at night is taken away by sleep, sexual intercourse or pleasure. In the day, the lifespan that is [spent] in the day is [used] for exertion toward wealth, or, when wealth has been obtained, for maintaining the family. The two particles “and” indicate the collection of what is not stated.

“But why would he expend his life for the sake of an impermanent family and so forth?” To this he replies. Although the body and the rest, the armies and accessories of the self, are unreal and falsely existent, he is heedlessly attached to them; although seeing their destruction through the example of the father and the like, he does not reflect on it.

Having stated the answer to the question concerning the contrary, he gives the answer to the question concerning what is to be heard and so forth with “therefore.” O Bhārata, descendant of Bharata. By “the self of all” he states [the Lord’s] being most beloved. By “Bhagavān,” beauty. By “Īśvara,” necessity. By “Hari,” the removal of bondage. “Fearlessness” means liberation, [desired] by one who desires it.

He says that there is no other higher good than this: this alone is the fruit, the gain of birth. He states it as “remembrance of Nārāyaṇa.” By saying that it is accomplished through Sāṅkhya and the like, he prevents their being gains through their own independence. Sāṅkhya is discrimination between the self and the not-self. Yoga is the eight-limbed [Yoga]. At the end, remembrance is the supreme gain; that is the meaning, for its greatness cannot be stated.

There he establishes good conduct as authority with “mainly.” [They are] withdrawn from injunction and prohibition through injunction and prohibition, and, although situated in Brahman beyond the qualities, it is well known.

“What is this unprecedented thing you are saying?” It is indeed unprecedented, he says. This Bhāgavata, spoken by Bhagavān, having His name alone as its principal subject, is a Purāṇa equal to Brahman and equal to all the Vedas. Or, it is that by which Brahman is rightly measured.

From where did you receive it? He says: “I studied.” From Dvaipāyana, my father. When? “At the beginning of Dvāpara”—in the end of Dvāpara, that is the meaning. The incarnation of Vyāsa is famous in the time of Śantanu and the like.
“Why would there be engagement in study for you who are perfected?” To this he says: “Even though perfectly established.” “Having attracted the mind” means having an attracted mind.

He says that for practitioners and perfected persons there is no other higher good than this: “this.” For those desiring [material enjoyment], this alone is the means for the respective fruits. For those becoming dispassionate, those desiring liberation, this alone is the means of liberation. For yogins, the knowers, this alone is determined as the fruit. There is no authority that needs to be stated here; that is the meaning.

“Only a little life remains; what shall I accomplish?” “Do not grieve,” he says, in three [verses]. “By years that are unnoticed” means by unmarked years. “Years” means years. “Known” means known to pass in vain. “By which” means by that knowledge. “One should strive” means one should make effort.

Khaṭvāṅga, while stationed on the side of the gods, defeated the demons. Then, when the pleased gods said, “Choose a boon,” he said, “First, tell me the measure of my life.” Then the gods said, “That is only a moment.” Then he came very quickly by aerial vehicle to the earth and took refuge in Hari. For this heavenly-earthly realm is rich in rajas. The earth is the field of action.
But for you, even now, at this present time. “So long” means with that amount of time; accomplish the other-worldly means.

There he speaks of dispassion with “at the end of life.” “Free from fear” means free from the fear of death. “Non-attachment” means absence of attachment. With that weapon he should cut desire for pleasure, and also desire for those who follow the body—sons, wife and the like.

Then, in the Second [Canto], after meditation on the gross [form], the mind having been conquered, it is said that it should be fixed on Viṣṇu, the witness of all and the Lord of all.

Thus the Vairāja meditation having a visible support has been described; here the meditation on the inner controller accomplished by it is stated.

Here, for now, he states the intermediate fruit of the previously mentioned meditation with “thus.” By that meditation, from satisfied Hari, Brahmā, having regained the remembrance of creation that had been lost before, at the time of dissolution, created this universe as it had been before the dissolution. He whose intelligence is resolute—therefore his vision is unfailing. Thus, through that meditation, the power to create the universe arises.

The meaning is that Brahmā, having obtained from pleased Hari the memory of the creation that had been lost at the time of dissolution, created this universe as it was before the dissolution.

Even one who is detached from the fruit of worship has eligibility for meditation on the pure self. Therefore, for the sake of dispassion, he censures all the fruit of action. The “sound-made Brahman” is the Veda. Its “path” is this way of understanding the fruit of action. What is it? By meaningless names alone—such as heaven—the practitioner’s intelligence meditates and makes the respective desires.

He states its meaninglessness itself: on a path made of māyā, lying as if asleep through the impression of happiness, seeing dreams and wandering, he does not obtain the objects. Even having reached that world, he does not attain blameless happiness; that is the meaning.

Then, anticipating the objection that, if the fruit of action were entirely abandoned, the body would immediately fall, he says this. “Therefore the wise person in names alone”: in names alone, whose need is only as much as is necessary for maintaining the body, he should be such a person. “Not heedless”: unattached even to that much. “Firm in understanding”: one who is certain that this is not happiness. Even then, when that need is accomplished in another way, seeing the labor involved in the effort there, he should not strive.

He explains accomplishment otherwise with two [verses], beginning with “when there is.” “Of a kaśipu” means of a bed. When the arm is naturally available, what need is there for head-rests? “In many ways” means in many kinds; “with the food-vessel” means with a vessel for eating.

“But the existence of the directions means simply nakedness; bark, food, water and a dwelling—how could these be obtained without the effort of begging?” To this he replies. “Barks” means pieces of cloth. “Those who support others” are the trees that nourish with fruits and the like. “Caves” are mountain ravines.

“But if sometimes these are unavailable, what is to be done?” To this he replies: does Ajita, Hari, not protect those who have approached and taken shelter? The word “what” is connected with the preceding [questions] as well. “By wealth”: he who is intoxicated by it; “blind”: those whose discrimination is destroyed.

“What then should he do?” Hari is to be served, he says: thus, being detached, he should worship Him. The reasons for His being worthy of worship are these: He is naturally established in one’s own mind. Because He is the self, He is therefore dear. And service of one who is dear is happiness itself. “Reality” means what is real, not false like the not-self. “Bhagavān” means endowed with qualities worthy of worship; He is also endless and eternal. Being of this nature, He should be worshiped.

“Of fixed meaning” means one whose true nature is certain. Being satisfied by the bliss of experiencing Him, his nature as happiness in itself is shown. Moreover, in that worship there is cessation, destruction, of ignorance, the cause of saṃsāra.

He strengthens this very point by censuring other thought: “who?” Neglecting that transcendental contemplation of the Supreme Hari, who, apart from materialistic animals, dull through action, would engage in thought of the nonpermanent? As the śruti says: “This one alone is an animal of the gods.” Seeing the people fallen into Vaitaraṇī, and there undergoing the afflictions born of their own actions, beginning with those pertaining to the self, who would do so? Vaitaraṇī is the river situated at the gate of Yama; saṃsāra is Vaitaraṇī because it is similar to it.

He states that same meditation, with its qualifications, in six [verses], beginning with “some.” Within one’s own body, in the heart; in the space that is there, residing. “Prādeśa” is the span between the index finger and the thumb; that alone is the measure, and therefore the measure of the heart is figuratively spoken of there. “Kañja” means lotus. “Rathāṅga” means wheel.

The śruti says: “The Person measuring a thumb, standing in the middle within the self” [Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.1.12]. In both passages, what is intended is the subtlety of the all-pervading [Lord] in relation to the lotus of the heart.

“Lotus” means a lotus; likewise, clear and wide are the eyes of Him whose eyes are so. The saffron filaments of a kadamba flower are yellow; likewise yellow are the garments of Him whose garments are so. Those golden armlets on which great jewels shine belong to Him. And those great jewels shine; His crown and earrings are made of them.

“Blooming” means opened. The whorl of the lotus of the heart is itself the abode, the place, and in that [place]. The lotus feet of Him whose feet have been placed there by the lords of yoga. “Śrī” itself is the mark, the sign; He is endowed with it. The possessive suffix na, expressing the meaning of possession, is prescribed after pāma and the like. He whose Kaustubha jewel is on the neck. He who is covered and pervaded by a forest garland, through the unfading beauty that is His.
The face that shines through a smile, on a countenance beautified by curls distinguished by smoothness and the like, is lovely.

Through that playful smile, which is not dejected but generous, and through the eyebrow movements that arise in that glance, abundant grace is indicated by Him. He is appearing through meditation, made of thought.

He states this very meditation with “one by one.” “He should experience” means he should meditate. Whatever limb—from the feet, ankles and so forth—has appeared by being conquered without effort, leaving that limb aside, he should hold and meditate on the next, the shank, knee and so forth. The intellect is purified in that [limb], or it becomes steady there.

“Purified” also means that the intellect abandons its attachment to sense objects.

He states that this meditation is an element of the previously mentioned Vairāja meditation with “as long as.” “The higher” are Brahmā and the rest; “the lower” are those from whom [the Lord is] higher. Why? Because He is the Lord of the universe, the seer, and not the seen, being a mass of consciousness. “Devotional service” is characterized by love. “At the end of action” means after performing the necessary duties. By this it is said that action too extends only up to devotional service. “Attentive” means devoted to the observance of the rule.

Thus, the duty of a person approaching death has been stated. Now he states the duty of that same person who desires to abandon the body himself, with four and a half verses beginning “steady.”

“O King,” when a renunciant of this nature desires to abandon this body, this world, then he should not attach the mind to a place, a sacred region, or to a time, such as the northern course of the sun. He should not become attached. For place and time are not causes of success for a yogin; Yoga alone is. Having become firmly certain of this, he should take up a steady and comfortable seat and control the life airs; that is the meaning.

In the Third [chapter], the excellence among Viṣṇu’s devotees is [described] for those hearing the sage; through an upsurge of devotion, reverent hearing of those acts is spoken.

Now, in order to state that the worship of other deities too has only a trifling fruit, like the worship of sons and the like, and is therefore to be abandoned, he repeats what was previously said with “thus.” “Me” means me. At some time, by the arrangement of fate, among living beings who have obtained human birth, among those who are thoughtful, and even among those who are dying, especially for these, this hearing of Hari’s topics and the like has been prescribed; that is the meaning.
“Brahmaṇaspati” is Brahmā, the lord of the Veda. One desiring acuity of the senses should worship Indra. One desiring progeny should worship the Prajāpatis, Dakṣa and the rest.
“Māyā” is Durgā. “Vibhāvasu” is fire. One desiring wealth is a seeker of wealth. “Power” means influence; one desiring that, being powerful, should worship the Rudras.

“Food and the like” means food that is to be eaten and chewed. “The sons of Aditi” are the twelve Ādityas. One desiring the independence of the subjects dwelling in the countries should worship the Sādhyas.
“Ilā” is the earth. “Stability” means not falling from one’s position. “Rodasī” means heaven and earth.
The Apsarās, and Urvaśī among them.

“Yajña” is Viṣṇu, qualified by sacrifice. “Treasury” is the accumulation of wealth. Here “one desiring wealth” differs in meaning by referring to wealth alone. “Conjugal relation” is mutual affection; that alone is the object of one for whom it is the purpose.

“The object of dharma” means one desiring dharma. “The Supreme Lord” is Viṣṇu, qualified by the highest praise. “Extending the thread” means seeking an increase of offspring. “Protection” is the removal of obstacles; one desiring that should worship the Puṇyajanas, the Yakṣas. “Strength” is power; one desiring that should worship the gods, the groups of Maruts.

“Kingdom” means kingship; one desiring that should worship the Manus, the gods who protect the Manvantaras. The kingdom that is the king’s activity—one desiring that should worship the Viśvadevas; this is the distinction. “Seeking victory over an enemy” means desiring the enemy’s death; one should worship Nirṛti, a demon. “Desiring desire” means desiring enjoyment. “Without desire” means desiring dispassion. “The Supreme Person” is the Lord, qualified by being distinct from Prakṛti.
“Without desire” means an exclusive devotee. Or, one who has all desires, stated and unstated, should worship the complete, unqualified Person.

By the worship of Indra and the other deities, through their respective worship, the fruit of devotional service is also stated through connection and difference. In this life, for those worshipping Indra and the others, by that respective worship, association with devotees of the Bhāgavata arises, and from that association an unwavering disposition toward Bhagavān, devotion, arises. This alone is the development, the gain, of the highest good, the supreme human aim. Everything else is trifling; that is the meaning.

“Through connection and difference” means through the distinctness of the relation. In the worship of each deity, the attainment of the particular fruit stated for that deity is “difference.” Through worship of each deity, destruction of sin gives association with the Bhāgavatas, and through that association unwavering devotion to Bhagavān arises; this is “connection”—a slight explanation. Or, connection and difference arise because one thing has both functions. Just as, in the statement “the sacrificial post is of khadira; for one desiring strength it is of khadira,” the one khadira post is both an element of the sacrifice and a means of strength, so here worship of the various deities is both a means of their respective fruits and a means of the fruit of devotion to Hari. Since it is a means for both fruits, Indra and the others should be worshipped with the desire for Hari’s devotion, not with another desire; that is the purport of the whole. Thus the cowherd maidens worshipped Kātyāyanī with the desire for Kṛṣṇa.

By “association with the Bhāgavatas” he praises the relish for Hari’s topics that is indicated: “knowledge.” In those narratives knowledge arises. What kind of knowledge? That from which the whirlpool, the mass of the waves of the qualities such as attachment, is withdrawn on every side. Moreover, immediately thereafter, self-satisfaction arises; and in those [narratives] non-attachment to the qualities, the objects, is the cause of serenity of mind. In the reading “in both,” non-attachment to the qualities exists here and in the next world. The path approved as liberation itself is devotional service. One is satisfied by the pleasure of hearing—or, alternatively, one is not satisfied elsewhere. Who would not develop relish for those narratives of Hari?

From “association with the Bhāgavatas,” the attainment of Hari’s topics is understood. The word “and the like” includes birth, death, grief, delusion, hunger and thirst. “Whirlpool” means falling again and again.
“Spoken” means said. “Ṛṣi” means one who sees the Supreme Brahman. “Kavi” means one thoroughly versed in the sound-Brahman.
The cause of the desire to hear is this: let there be, in the assembly of the devotees, those narratives in which the discussion of Hari itself is the later fruit.
He elaborates this with two [verses], beginning with “he indeed.” [He is] the one who accepted play in the form of worship of Kṛṣṇa and the like.
